desc:
The text s contains lowercase letters and the wildcard character ?. Each ? can be replaced by any lowercase letter you like, independently of the other wildcards. The pattern p has only lowercase letters.

Count the substrings of s of length p.length that can be turned, by choosing replacements for their wildcards, into an anagram of p. Count by start position.

s = "a?cb?", p = "abc"
a?c -> ? becomes b: abc   yes
?cb -> ? becomes a: acb   yes
cb? -> ? becomes a: cba   yes
result = 3
s = "aa?b", p = "abc"
aa? has two a's but p has only one -> no
a?b -> yes
result = 1
constraints: s consists of lowercase letters and '?'
hints: Compare with the plain anagram-window problem: what changes when a window contains wildcards?
A wildcard can supply any letter that p needs. The window fails only when it has too many copies of some real letter, more than p contains.
Because the window and p have the same length, a window works exactly when no letter has window count greater than its count in p. Track how many letters currently have an excess.
editorial: Let need[c] be the count of letter c in p and have[c] the count of that real letter in the window; wildcards are not counted in have. If every have[c] <= need[c], then the real letters use up part of p and the remaining positions are exactly the wildcards (both the window and p have length m), so each wildcard can be replaced by one of the still-needed letters. If some letter has have[c] > need[c], no replacement can fix it, because replacing wildcards cannot remove a real letter.

So keep excess, the number of letters with have[c] > need[c], and update it in O(1) when a letter enters (count goes from need to need + 1: excess + 1) or leaves (from need + 1 to need: excess - 1). Ignore '?' characters when updating. Count windows where excess == 0. Time O(n + m), space O(1).
